about: What a balance pass is allowed to change about each spell, and what each spell is for. Read data/balance/README.md before editing. This file is authoring metadata: the data builder never reads it, so it does not touch the content hash.

mirror.reads: Both sides play the content equally well, so everything left is the content.

skill.reads: Playing well still beats playing at random. A change that closes this gap has removed the decisions instead of balancing them.

variety.reads: Whether the content offers a choice, which is a different question from whether a greedy bot takes one. Both sides play greedily four decisions in five and draw uniformly the fifth (ADR 0014), so a spell the argmax always passes over still gets cast and can be read. Every target that needs a spell to be cast in order to mean anything is read here rather than on the mirrored run.

exploit.reads: How far a player who only wants to win gets against the way the game is meant to be played. Greedy is the taste this catalogue is balanced for; agent A is a searched set that shares none of it and beats Greedy anyway. Content where the two are far apart is content that punishes playing it the intended way. Agent A goes stale when the content moves — a tuning pass changes what there is to exploit — so it is refreshed from the next search run, not kept.

objective.score: Sum over the targets of weight * (distance outside the band / scale) ** 2. Zero is on target, lower is better. Metric names are report.json's, so a target and a report row are the same number; spellUsageShare, spellsNeverCast and spellsBarelyCast are the ones the tuner adds, because they need the catalogue and not only the evaluation. A candidate that breaks a constraint is not scored at all. Adding spellsBarelyCast made every score before it incomparable with every score after it: a run reading 40.45 under the old set is not a better run than one reading 41 under this one. ADR 0029 did it again, and harder: seven targets moved off the mirrored run onto the exploring one without their bands changing, which took the core content from 69.39 to 52.00 without a single number in the content moving. Compare scores only across runs judged by the same set read from the same runs.

targets.why: Identical agents, so anything away from one half is the content favouring a slot. 64.0% at the last measured run, down from 81.5% when spell initiative got priced.
A draw is the round cap arriving before either team can finish the other.
Long enough that a bad round can be traded back, short enough that the cap of 30 stays out of reach. 5.8 at the last measured run: the catalogue currently kills faster than it lets anyone react.
Matches that run out of rounds mean neither side can convert, usually stacked permanent defense.

Agent A's share of declarations that fizzled. Both agents are the same in a mirrored run, so A is the content's own rate. Mostly targets dying before the action resolves, so it falls on its own as matches lengthen. 21.4% at the last measured run.

Bits over agent A's declared spells. 2.21 at the last measured run over ten distinct spells, of a possible 5.17 over thirty-six. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029), where it reads 2.530 against 1.992 on a mirrored greedy run: the difference was the argmax passing spells over, not the content failing to offer them.

The largest share of landed casts any one spell takes across the whole catalogue. Since tierUsageShare reads the same thing per tier and catches what this one hides — a tier fully monopolised by a spell that is small in the total — this stays as the coarse guard and carries half the weight. 0.855 on the core content. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029), where it reads 0.410 against 0.478 on a mirrored greedy run: the difference was the argmax passing spells over, not the content failing to offer them.

Spells in the catalogue that no declaration ever landed. Needs the catalogue as well as the evaluation, so the tuner computes it. The band is read against what the build carries, not against what is on disk: on the nine-spell core content two spells failing to come up is slack, twelve would be the whole game. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029), where it reads 0 against 2 on a mirrored greedy run: the difference was the argmax passing spells over, not the content failing to offer them.

Spells taking under 1% of the landed casts of the tier they are offered in. The hole spellsNeverCast leaves: pummel took 6 of 5283 landed casts of a mirrored run, which is dead in every sense that decides a game and is not a zero, so a buff that moved it from 4 casts to 6 read as no change at all. Read against the tier rather than the catalogue because a tier is the set a player chooses between at one moment. Counts strictly the spells spellsNeverCast does not: a zero is a zero in either reading, and with the same band and weight on both, counting it twice would quietly double what the objective asks of that one case. A run whose content carries no tiers reports this as missing rather than as zero. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029), where it reads 0 against 1 on a mirrored greedy run: the difference was the argmax passing spells over, not the content failing to offer them.

The largest share of landed casts any one spell takes among the spells of its own tier, worst tier. A tier is the set a player chooses between at one moment, so this is the balance they actually feel. Uniform is 1/n: 0.33 for the three starting spells, 0.17 for the six of tier 1. It reads 1.000 on the core content — heavy_strike takes every landed cast of tier 0 — where the catalogue-wide share reads 0.855 and hides it. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029), where it reads 0.568 against 0.742 on a mirrored greedy run: the difference was the argmax passing spells over, not the content failing to offer them.

How many times harder the best damaging spell of a tier hits per landed cast than the worst, worst tier. Which spells count is read from the content — does the spell carry a Damage effect — never from what its casts landed, so lowering an attack until its hits are all absorbed widens this reading instead of dropping the spell out of it. A heal is not compared: it shares no unit with an attack. The ratio is floored at half a point of damage per cast and capped at 5. 2.41 on the core content. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029), where it reads 5.000, the same as on a mirrored greedy run. That sameness is what says this one is the content and not the agent.

The gap between the best and the worst win share among the spells of a tier, worst tier, counting only spells enough sides declared. Two spells offered together should not be worth wildly different results. 0.262 on the core content. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029), where it reads 0.148 against 0.322 on a mirrored greedy run: the difference was the argmax passing spells over, not the content failing to offer them.
The skill gap. Content that a random agent can hold has stopped asking anything.

A guard, not a push. It reads 0.55 today — 220 of 400 — and the 95% interval on 400 matches is about a twentieth either way, so asking for less than this would be asking the tuner to chase noise. What it stops is the tuner widening the gap, which nothing else here can see: every other target reads a mirrored run, where both sides play the same way and an exploit is invisible by construction. Read it with the skill target, which refuses the degenerate answer — flattening the game closes this gap and fails that one.

noNewStrictDominance.what: A candidate may not add a pair where one spell is strictly better than another: same targeting origin, at least as many targets, cost no higher, Spell initiative no lower, critical chance no lower, every effect at least as large, and strictly better on one of them.
noNewStrictDominance.why: A spell three nodes down the tree outclassing a starting spell is what progression means, so the pairs the catalogue already has are not defects to remove. Adding one is: it takes a decision out of a hand that had it. Journal entry ci-9 spent a whole learning investigation discovering the starting kit was shaped that way.

noIndistinguishableSpells.what: No two spells may carry the same cost, Spell initiative, critical chance, targeting and effects. The same signature the engine's Spell.Indistinguishable audit compares.
noIndistinguishableSpells.why: The engine plays both, but no result can attribute anything to either, so tuning one moves nothing the other does not.

startingKitOffersAChoice.what: None of the three spells every creature starts with may be strictly better than another. Implied by noNewStrictDominance, named separately because this is the one hand every match is dealt.
startingKitOffersAChoice.why: Journal entry ci-9: heavy_strike was strictly better than basic_attack, and no learner could find a decision that was not there.

spell:wait.name: Wait
spell:wait.intent: The floor of the game: spend the activation on nothing and come back one energy richer. It is what a creature does when everything it knows is too expensive, so it must stay free and it must stay worse than acting.
keep: Free to cast
Never worth more than an attack the creature can already afford
spell:wait.note: Spell initiative is not a knob here: a starting spell does not grant it (ADR 0017), and this is one of the three the creature already knows.

spell:basic_attack.name: Basic Attack
spell:basic_attack.intent: The reliable jab of the starting kit: cheap, certain, no critical. Every other attack in the catalogue is priced against its damage per energy, so moving it moves everything.
keep: The cheapest damaging spell a creature knows on round one
No critical chance: it is the predictable one
spell:basic_attack.note: Spell initiative is not a knob here: a starting spell does not grant it (ADR 0017).

spell:heavy_strike.name: Heavy Strike
spell:heavy_strike.intent: The starting kit's commitment: pay more of the round for the bigger opening hit. The decision it exists to pose is spend now or bank for later, so it has to cost what it wins.
keep: Strictly dearer and stronger than Basic Attack, never both cheaper and better
The reason a first round has a choice in it
spell:heavy_strike.note: Spell initiative is not a knob here: a starting spell does not grant it (ADR 0017).

spell:pummel.name: Pummel
spell:pummel.intent: The Brawler's cheap swing: one energy for a hit that crits two times in three. It buys tempo rather than a big number, and the critical chance is the whole reason to take it over Basic Attack.
keep: At most one energy dearer than Basic Attack
Its critical chance stays its defining stat
spell:pummel.note: check-knobs reports this spell as outclassed, and raising its own bounds is not the way out. At 4 damage it would be strictly better than Lightning Bolt -- same damage, same critical chance, one energy cheaper -- so noNewStrictDominance refuses it, and a wider bound here would only buy candidates the constraints throw away. Measured: its whole box tops out around 5.4 against Lightning Bolt's 6.7, and even a certain critical at 3 damage reaches 6.2. Its other edge, costing 1 against 2, is worth nothing on this rule set: 0 of 319 traced declarations had the caster below 2 energy, so the cost never binds. Making this spell a choice is a move on the pair -- Lightning Bolt down as this one comes up -- which is a two-spell candidate, so neither the sweep nor the paired opening can build it and only the climb can. That is what the search budget is for.

spell:guard.name: Guard
spell:guard.intent: The Brawler's investment: a point of defense on an ally for good, plus a point while the pressure is on. Cheap, repeatable and permanent, which makes it the likeliest single cause of a match no one can finish.
keep: Half of it is permanent and stacks on every cast
Cheaper than any healing spell: it prevents, it does not repair

spell:protective_slam.name: Protective Slam
spell:protective_slam.intent: The Mercenary's opener, and the branch's answer to armour. Legacy gave its caster a point of defense, which the taxonomy cannot express: a spell has one target origin, so hitting an enemy and protecting an ally are two spells. Protection is expressed as tempo instead -- a slammed enemy acts later -- which is the one protective thing that can be said to an enemy. That also gives it teeth a bigger hit would not have: defense absorbs damage and does nothing to a stagger, so this is what a Brawler stacking Guard and Full Plate is answered with.
keep: Protection through tempo, never armour: it always carries an initiative debuff
Reads as a trade, not a nuke
The stagger is the point; the damage only has to be worth the activation
spell:protective_slam.note: Most of its value was damage on purpose, because the initiative weight was 0.5 on reasoning alone (ADR 0018) and a version built mainly on the debuff would have rested on an unmeasured number. That objection is now spent: ADR 0032 swept the weight alone and moved it to 2.1, and the debuff half of this spell is what moved with it -- 1.6% of the mirror's casts to 7.0%, without a number here changing. The shape is worth revisiting deliberately rather than by default: at 2.1 the debuff is no longer the cheap half.

spell:chain_slash.name: Chain Slash
spell:chain_slash.intent: The Mercenary's payoff: the most damage any single cast puts on the board, split over two enemies. It is the reason to walk that line to the end, so it should stay expensive and stay late.
keep: Hits at most two: it is a cleave, not a storm
The largest cast in the catalogue

spell:thundering_seal.name: Thundering Seal
spell:thundering_seal.intent: Guard grown up: two permanent points of defense on an ally and two more for the round. The damage it used to send back to the attacker was not carried over (ADR 0012), so what is left is pure stacking mitigation.
keep: Stronger and dearer than Guard
The permanent half stacks on every cast

spell:full_plate.name: Full Plate
spell:full_plate.intent: Armour the Warlord is meant to always wear. Nothing implements passives yet, so it is a self-targeted permanent point of defense that can be cast every single round, and permanent plus repeatable is only bounded by what it costs. It costs one energy for that reason: half a round's income per point, so a creature that armours itself is a creature not attacking, which is the trade the spell should be.
keep: Plate, not a shirt: one cast is armour a creature can feel, and it stacks by being cast again
Never free: a permanent effect nobody pays for has no brake but the round cap
Cheap enough to cast in the rounds that decide the match, or it is not armour
spell:full_plate.note: Its price is the whole design and the reason its lower bound is one rather than zero. The spell is `SpellType.Passive` in a model where nothing implements a passive, so it is castable, repeatable and permanent; at zero it was unbounded and read 0.65 against the bolt's 6.47, which is how it went 400 matches without a single cast while being the most dangerous spell in the catalogue. Raising the permanent horizon would not have found that -- every reading prices one cast, and one point of defense is one point at any horizon. When a passive becomes a real always-on modifier, this entry is the first to revisit.

spell:restorative_gush.name: Restorative Gush
spell:restorative_gush.intent: The big single-target heal: more health back than most single hits take away. It decides on its own whether a war of attrition is winnable, which is why the average match length moves with it.
keep: Heals more in one cast than anything else
Single target: the team heals belong to the Trickster and the Shaman
spell:restorative_gush.note: Its critical chance is not a knob: the multiplier applies to damage only, and this spell deals none.

spell:crushing_stomp.name: Crushing Stomp
spell:crushing_stomp.intent: The Warlord's hammer and the costliest spell in the game: heavy damage and a round of the target doing nothing. Losing an activation is the harshest thing that can happen to a creature, so the price is the point of the spell.
keep: The most expensive cast in the catalogue
Damage and stun together, or it is just an expensive hit

spell:enraged_charge.name: Enraged Charge
spell:enraged_charge.intent: The Berserker's gamble, and the one spell in the catalogue whose whole point is the roll. One heavy swing at the highest critical chance anywhere, bought at a price that keeps it to every other round: rage that lands or does not, rather than a steady beat. It is what the class is offered before it is offered anything reliable.
keep: One swing, not a flurry: the roll is the spell, and two effects only split it
The highest critical chance in the catalogue, or it is just an expensive hit
Expensive enough that it cannot be the every-round attack
spell:enraged_charge.note: It reads big per cast on purpose and must be read per round instead: at three energy against an income of two it comes up every other round, so 12.60 a cast is 8.40 a round against `protective_slam`'s 7.33 at two energy. Read per cast it looks like twice the bolt; read per round it is fifteen percent over the spell beside it, which is what a tier-2 opener should be. Its own history is the warning: at 7.00 a cast it was 4.67 a round and fell from 122 landed casts to 32 the moment something at two energy arrived.

spell:tornado.name: Tornado
spell:tornado.intent: The cheapest sweep in the game: against a full team it is the best damage per energy anywhere. Its cost is the first place to look when matches end too quickly.
keep: The cheapest spell that reaches three enemies
Its efficiency comes from breadth, not from the size of the hit

spell:psycho_rush.name: Psycho Rush
spell:psycho_rush.intent: The Berserker's all-in: close to half a creature in a single cast. The two points of defense it used to cost its caster are not in the taxonomy, so it is a nuke with no downside and its price is doing all the work.
keep: The line's gamble: big, single target, expensive
Priced as if the recoil existed, because one day it will

spell:poison_slash.name: Poison Slash
spell:poison_slash.intent: The Scoundrel's signature: a small hit that keeps hurting. It is the cheapest way into bleed and the spell that teaches a player what a lasting effect is.
keep: The bleed is the point, the damage is the garnish
The entry-level bleed: weaker than Mortal Wound on every axis
spell:poison_slash.note: These bounds contain a good answer and it is in the interior, not at a corner -- but the measurements below were taken on the Brawler-buffed catalogue of the studio/content branch, where this spell carries a bleed of 1 per round over 2 rounds and Pummel carries 3 damage. This branch carries 1 over 1, so read them as the shape of the curve and not as this catalogue's numbers. There, at 2 damage: 1 over 2 is 6 landed casts; 2 over 2 is 59, still nothing; 2 over 3 takes 5155 of about 8900 with matches at 11.3 rounds, no draw and nothing at the round cap; 3 over 2 reaches the same usage with 12.5% draws; and the corner, 3 over 3, is worse than the middle at 2600, because it kills so fast that a match is 6.0 rounds and there are half as many casts to take a share of. The middle point takes the top spell's share of landed casts from 0.778 to 0.578. On this branch the same spell is at 3 landed casts, and one same-direction pair of steps from 1 over 1 lands on 2 over 2, which measures 310 casts of about 6150 -- fifty times better and still not the interior point, which is two steps of the duration away. Whether the objective keeps that first pair is its own question.

spell:throwing_star.name: Throwing Star
spell:throwing_star.intent: One energy for a small hit, and two points of Base initiative when it is unlocked: the Scoundrel buys speed by learning to throw. Its Spell initiative is worth more to the class than its damage.
keep: One energy: it is the cheap attack the class is priced around
Unlocking it is a tempo decision, not a damage one

spell:parasite_jab.name: Parasite Jab
spell:parasite_jab.intent: The Leech's opener and the first spell in the catalogue that feeds its caster (ADR 0031): a modest bite that puts some of what it takes back into whoever threw it. It is deliberately the weaker attack of its tier and the only one that answers being hurt, so the choice it offers is not how hard to hit but whether you need the health.
keep: It always feeds its caster: the bite is the price of the meal, not the point of it
A worse attack than the tier's attacks: the healing is what it is for
Never more healing than a real heal: it is a bite, not a Restorative Gush
spell:parasite_jab.note: The reading that matters is not in the numbers: `ActionScorer.HealScore` counts only the health a target is missing, so at full health this spell is worth its damage alone -- 4.50 against `lightning_bolt`'s 6.47 -- and only passes it once its caster has three points to get back. That is lifesteal's whole feel, and it is emergent rather than authored: a Leech reaches for this when it is hurt and for something else when it is not. `cast_value` cannot see the condition and prices the healing whole, so it reads 6.90 where play reads between 4.50 and 6.90.

spell:hateful_sacrifice.name: Hateful Sacrifice
spell:hateful_sacrifice.intent: The largest single hit in the game, and it was meant to cost the caster four health. Without that self-damage the energy price is the only thing paying for it.
keep: The heaviest single-target hit
Its price stands in for the missing self-damage

spell:soul_devourer.name: Soul Devourer
spell:soul_devourer.intent: The worst rate in the catalogue, because the energy it used to drain from the target was dropped. It exists as a node on the Leech line rather than as a spell anyone should want, and fixing the price comes before making it hit harder.
keep: Waiting on an energy-drain effect
Cheaper before it is stronger

spell:momentum.name: Momentum
spell:momentum.intent: Wait's opposite trade, and the spell whose name finally says what it does: Wait hands over energy now, Momentum builds it, a point at the start of each of the next few rounds. The Assassin spends the same activation and comes out ahead if the match lasts, behind if it does not -- and permanently faster either way, because its Spell initiative of three is the highest in the catalogue.
keep: Free, like Wait, and it is the same activation: the trade is when the energy arrives, not what it costs
It builds rather than hands over: the day it gives energy on the spot it is Wait again
Its Spell initiative is half of what it is for
spell:momentum.note: The first spell to use `EnergyRegeneration`, which ADR 0020 added and deliberately left unused, naming Momentum as one of the two candidates. Do not read its bounds as a route to making it castable: at 0.2 a point of energy the top of this box is 1.60 an activation against an attack's 6-and-up, so `check-knobs` reports it against `full_plate` and will keep reporting it. That finding is right and the way out it names is the other one -- the rival's bounds, or the price of energy, which ADR 0020 set and nothing has ever tuned. Widening this spell until it clears the bar would mean handing out twenty points of energy.

spell:death_squad.name: Death Squad
spell:death_squad.intent: Energy spent to give the whole team energy: a small net gain and a tempo swing for three creatures at once. It stands in for the initiative and critical buff the taxonomy cannot express, so read it as haste rather than as a battery.
keep: Costs more than any one ally receives
Team-wide, or it is Momentum with extra steps

spell:mortal_wound.name: Mortal Wound
spell:mortal_wound.intent: The bleed that actually kills: a hit now and a heavier wound over the rounds that follow. It is the reason to fear the Assassin and the likeliest single cause of a match that runs away from the loser.
keep: More damage over time than up front
The catalogue's heaviest bleed

spell:noxious_cure.name: Noxious Cure
spell:noxious_cure.intent: The cure is noxious to the cured: the whole team is mended and the whole team is slowed for having drunk it. Legacy stripped 2 defense from the allies it healed, which the taxonomy cannot say -- `DefenseBuff.Of` refuses anything below 1, so there is no negative buff -- and the substitution is the one `infectious_blast` already uses, a defense shred rendered as the single stat debuff that exists. The bargain is the spell: without a cost it is a free team heal, and the Trickster is the class that makes you pay for things.
keep: Team-wide heal: it reaches the team or it is Rejuvenate
It always slows the allies it heals: the price is paid by the cured, which is what makes it noxious
Never enough slow to be worth casting on an enemy: this is a cure, not a weapon
spell:noxious_cure.note: Its critical chance is not a knob: the multiplier applies to damage only and this spell deals none. Two readings the numbers hide. `HealScore` counts only the health an ally is missing, so on a whole team this is worth nothing and it is never a free cast. And the debuff is a **cost** although it is written like any other effect -- the targeting origin is what says so, and both `cast_value` and `dominates` had to be taught it: read unsigned, slowing the allies you heal made this spell read as strictly better than a plain heal of the same size.

spell:tranquilizer_dart.name: Tranquilizer Dart
spell:tranquilizer_dart.intent: The cheap stun: a modest hit and a stolen activation for less than Crushing Stomp asks. The Trickster buys the tempo the Warlord pays full price for, and pays for it in damage.
keep: Cheaper than Crushing Stomp and weaker for it
The stun is the spell

spell:infectious_blast.name: Infectious Blast
spell:infectious_blast.intent: The only spell that neither damages nor heals: one energy to slow the whole enemy team. It was a defense shred and is approximated with the one debuff the taxonomy has, which makes it the game's only pure tempo play.
keep: No damage: it is control or it is nothing
The cheapest thing that touches all three enemies

spell:lightning_bolt.name: Lightning Bolt
spell:lightning_bolt.intent: The Sorcerer's bread and butter: a modest hit that crits two times in three. It is the caster's mirror of Pummel and the spell every Sorcerer branch gets compared against.
keep: The class's baseline attack: everything deeper in the tree must beat it
spell:lightning_bolt.note: Its price is the open question of this catalogue, so the cost bound is wider than most. At two energy it takes 85% of the landed casts on the core content; at three it takes 36%, matches run 9.5 rounds instead of 8.1, and the objective falls from 104.1 to 19.4. Nothing says three is the end of that curve, so the knob reaches four. Its critical chance was listed here as its identity until a measurement showed the identity does not distinguish it: Pummel carries the same 0.667, and a critical multiplies base damage, so at equal rates it widens the gap it is supposed to close. Against a Pummel at 3 damage, dropping this spell's chance to 0.417 leaves Pummel 448 landed casts of about 5900, 0.317 leaves it 649, and one in six flips the catalogue: Pummel 4986, this spell 754, and eight spells cast instead of seven. The cost is length -- 7.6, 9.2 and 11.3 rounds, with the round-cap share 0.000, 0.045 and 0.100 against a band of 0.05 -- so the objective has a real trade to arbitrate, and none of that range was reachable at a floor of 0.4. What makes this a Sorcerer spell rather than a Brawler one is deliberately left unstated: the critical chance no longer says it, and the answer is a design decision rather than a bound.

spell:rejuvenate.name: Rejuvenate
spell:rejuvenate.intent: The cheapest healing in the game and the reason a Sorcerer team can outlast a Brawler team. Its price sets the whole healing line: every other heal has to justify costing more than this one.
keep: The cheapest heal
Single target
spell:rejuvenate.note: Its critical chance is not a knob: the multiplier applies to damage only, and this spell deals none.

spell:meteor.name: Meteor
spell:meteor.intent: The Wizard's sweep, and the spell that says what reach costs: each enemy takes less than one of them would take from a single-target spell of the same depth, and the whole line is worth more than any of them. It opens the class whose three spells are all about reach, so it is the one that has to make the trade legible -- a sweep that hit as hard per target as a bolt would simply be a bolt that hits three.
keep: Reaches three enemies
Each of them takes less than a single-target spell of its tier deals: reach is paid for per target
The strongest thing in its tier, but by a step and not by half again
spell:meteor.note: Its bounds used to defer to Tornado -- 'these two are priced against each other or one of them is dead content' -- and Tornado is a tier deeper and disabled, so this spell was deferring its numbers to one nobody can cast while it became the ceiling of its own tier. Read per round, four damage on three targets was 12.00 against `enraged_charge`'s 8.40, 43% clear of everything; three is 9.00, a step ahead rather than a different game. The damage floor drops to 2 so a real per-target discount is reachable, and the cap to 4 so it can never hit as hard per target as `lightning_bolt` does on one. When Tornado is enabled the comparison comes back, and it is a comparison between two sweeps rather than a reason to leave this one unpriced.

spell:engulfing_flames.name: Engulfing Flames
spell:engulfing_flames.intent: Psycho Rush in a robe: as written today it carries the same cost, the same damage, the same critical chance and the same targeting. Two spells that identical cannot both be interesting, and no evaluation can attribute anything to either.
keep: Must stop being a copy of Psycho Rush
The Wizard's single-target answer to its own sweep

spell:ice_spear.name: Ice Spear
spell:ice_spear.intent: Damage that also slows: a hit now and initiative off the target for a round. It is the Wizard's answer to going second and the only offensive spell that touches the timeline.
keep: Damage and slow in one cast
A rate spell, not a nuke: it wins the next round, not this one

spell:summon_minions.name: Summon Minions
spell:summon_minions.intent: The only cast in the catalogue that does nothing when it lands: the minions are raised, and they gnaw at the whole enemy line over the rounds that follow. Raising them is paid in the Necromancer's own health, so the class opens on a bargain rather than on a blow -- patience bought with life. It is what both its children inherit: `crazed_specter`'s reach and `revenant_guards`' willingness to pay.
keep: Nothing lands now: every point of its damage is deferred, which is what makes it a summon and not an attack
It is paid in the summoner's own health, never in anyone else's
It reaches the whole enemy line: one minion each, not three on one
spell:summon_minions.note: Two firsts, and they are the design: no other spell defers all of its damage, and no other spell charges its caster health (ADR 0031). It used to be `EnergyGain 3` for 2, an approximation of the minions the two spells behind it spent -- and ADR 0020 named it as one of the two candidates for `EnergyRegeneration`. That nomination is declined here, with a measurement: energy is 0.2 a point, so an energy spell tops out around 1.60 an activation against an attack's 6 and up, and `momentum` was measured cast 0 times at `explore:0.2` and 8 at `explore:0.5` after being given exactly that treatment. Two energy openers would have been two dead openers. It was then briefly `DefenseBuff 1` for two rounds on three allies, which measured fine and read as nothing: a smaller `revenant_guards`, the spell it is supposed to open rather than rehearse.

spell:revenant_guards.name: Revenant Guards
spell:revenant_guards.intent: Thundering Seal for the whole team at the same price: permanent defense on three allies at once. Cast every round it makes a team unkillable, which makes it the clearest thing in this catalogue that needs a rule rather than a number.
keep: Team-wide and permanent: the strongest defensive cast in the game
Priced above the single-target version or it simply replaces it
spell:revenant_guards.note: Its critical chance is not a knob: the multiplier applies to damage only, and this spell deals none.
